overview: Iraq is a country in Western Asia. Its capital and largest city is Baghdad. The land between its two great rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates, was ancient Mesopotamia, where some of the world's first cities and earliest writing developed. Iraq has large oil reserves. Arabic and Kurdish are official languages, and the Kurdistan Region in the north has its own government.

geography.text: The Tigris and Euphrates flow from the north-west to the south-east and join before reaching the Persian Gulf along Iraq's short coastline. The land between them is fertile, while the west is desert. The north-east rises into the Zagros mountains, and the marshes of the south are among the largest wetlands in the Middle East.

history.text: In ancient Mesopotamia the Sumerians built some of the first cities and invented writing, and later Babylon became a great capital. Baghdad was the centre of the Islamic world under the Abbasid caliphs. After Ottoman and British rule, Iraq became independent in 1932. Saddam Hussein ruled from 1979 until a US-led invasion in 2003, which was followed by years of conflict.

events.title: Writing invented
events.text: Sumerians develop cuneiform, one of the first writing systems.

events.title: Hammurabi's laws
events.text: The king of Babylon sets out one of the earliest written law codes.

events.title: Baghdad founded
events.text: The Abbasid caliph founds Baghdad, which becomes a centre of learning.

events.title: Independence
events.text: Iraq becomes independent from British rule.

government.text: Iraq is a federal parliamentary republic. Voters elect the Council of Representatives, which chooses the President, who then names a Prime Minister. By custom, the Prime Minister is a Shia Arab, the President a Kurd and the Speaker a Sunni Arab. The Kurdistan Region in the north has its own government.

economy.text: Oil makes up almost all of Iraq's exports and most of government income. It has some of the world's largest reserves. Wars and conflict have damaged its infrastructure, and the government is the largest employer.

culture.text: Ancient Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, was the birthplace of writing, cities and the wheel. Babylon and Ur are among its famous ancient sites. Baghdad was a centre of science and learning in the Middle Ages, home to the House of Wisdom.

items.title: Babylon
items.text: Ancient capital of Hammurabi and Nebuchadnezzar.

items.title: Ziggurat of Ur
items.text: A stepped temple more than 4,000 years old.

items.title: The marshes
items.text: Wetlands of southern Iraq, home to the Marsh Arabs, listed by UNESCO.

sport.text: Football is Iraq's most popular sport. In 2007, during a time of war, Iraq won the Asian Cup, uniting the country in celebration. Iraq also won the Arabian Gulf Cup in 2023.

items.text: Gulf Cup champions on home soil in Basra.

didYouKnow: The first known writing, cuneiform, was developed in what is now Iraq.
The wheel was used in Mesopotamia around 3500 BC.

keyPeople.name: Hammurabi
keyPeople.text: Wrote one of the first law codes.

keyPeople.name: Zaha Hadid
keyPeople.text: Born in Baghdad; the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize.
